claim: Acoustic overexposure and aging can damage auditory synapses in the inner ear by a process known as synaptopathy.

claim: A connection between sensory transduction and synaptopathy has not been established.

claim: Inner hair cell synapses were assessed in mice lacking Tmc1, Tmc2, or both.

claim: Inner hair cell synapses were assessed in Beethoven mice which carry a dominant Tmc1 mutation.

claim: Loss of synapses occurs in the absence of sensory transduction.

claim: Loss of IHC-SGN synapses is evident following noise exposure producing both temporary threshold shifts (TTS) and permanent threshold shifts (PTS).
source: Loss of IHC-SGN synapses, known as cochlear synaptopathy, is evident following noise exposure producing both temporary threshold shifts (TTS) and permanent threshold shifts (PTS), with rapid loss of up to 40–50% of synapses and gradual degeneration of SGNs even in the absence of hair cell death (Kujawa and Liberman, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kujawa and Liberman, 2009.

claim: Rapid loss of up to 40–50% of synapses occurs following noise exposure even in the absence of hair cell death.
source: Loss of IHC-SGN synapses, known as cochlear synaptopathy, is evident following noise exposure producing both temporary threshold shifts (TTS) and permanent threshold shifts (PTS), with rapid loss of up to 40–50% of synapses and gradual degeneration of SGNs even in the absence of hair cell death (Kujawa and Liberman, 2009).

claim: Gradual degeneration of SGNs occurs following noise exposure even in the absence of hair cell death.
